overviewSummary.sv: The change turns `Link.connect` from a single pass-through to `Transport.open` into a retry loop. It tries up to `maxAttempts` times (default 3) and waits longer after each failure (100 ms, then 200 ms, and so on). It now resolves to an `Outcome` ('connected' or 'gave-up') instead of a boolean. It also adds a one-shot 'settled' callback, registered with `whenSettled`. `settle` delivers it on a later timer tick. `startSession` now takes a `report` function. It registers a settled callback that reports 'session ready' or 'offline mode', and it reports 'retrying later' right away when `connect` gives up.

overview.sv:
The change turns `Link.connect` from a single pass-through to `Transport.open` into a retry loop. It tries up to `maxAttempts` times (default 3) and waits longer after each failure (100 ms, then 200 ms, and so on). It now resolves to an `Outcome` ('connected' or 'gave-up') instead of a boolean. It also adds a one-shot 'settled' callback, registered with `whenSettled`. `settle` delivers it on a later timer tick. `startSession` now takes a `report` function. It registers a settled callback that reports 'session ready' or 'offline mode', and it reports 'retrying later' right away when `connect` gives up.

There are two kinds of reporting in `startSession`. One comes from the awaited return value of `connect`. The other comes from the settled callback, which `settle` schedules with `setTimeout(..., 0)`. That callback runs on a later event-loop task, after `connect` has already resolved. So when every attempt fails, 'retrying later' is reported before 'offline mode'. When the link connects, 'session ready' is reported after `startSession` may already have returned.

The repository has no tests for this code, and none of its own code calls `startSession`, so the new required `report` parameter breaks no caller here. The walks describe code that was read, not run.

title.sv: startSession registers a settled callback, then connects
title.en: startSession registers a settled callback, then connects

summary.sv: The session takes a report function, registers a settled callback and awaits connect.
summary.en: The session takes a report function, registers a settled callback and awaits connect.

body.sv:
`startSession` is where the walk starts. It now takes a `report` function, and it gives that function to two different paths:

1. **The settled callback.** `link.whenSettled(...)` only registers a callback here and does not run it. Later, the callback turns the `Outcome` into `'session ready'` or `'offline mode'`. The `Link` decides when it runs.
2. **The awaited result.** `await link.connect(address)` gives back an `Outcome` (`'connected' | 'gave-up'`), and `startSession` checks that value itself on the lines that follow.

In the old version, `startSession` had no `report` parameter. It awaited `connect` and ignored the `boolean` that came back, so nothing was reported.

**What to carry forward: one connection attempt can now reach `report` through both paths, and each path runs on its own timing.** The rest of this walk follows the order in which they fire. The next step shows that `whenSettled` keeps only one callback, so registering a second one replaces the first.

details.sv:
Each path covers different outcomes. The callback has a message for both `'connected'` and `'gave-up'`. The direct check acts only on `'gave-up'`, where it reports `'retrying later'`. So with `'connected'`, only the callback reports anything. With `'gave-up'`, both paths report.

`report` is a required parameter, so any existing caller written for the old two-argument signature no longer compiles. No other caller of `startSession` exists in either revision.

summary.sv: The callback goes into the onSettled field, replacing any earlier one.
summary.en: The callback goes into the onSettled field, replacing any earlier one.

body.sv:
This step follows the `whenSettled` call in `startSession`. All `whenSettled` does is store the callback in the private `onSettled` field. Nothing runs yet, and nothing here checks the link's state.

**`onSettled` holds at most one callback.** A second `whenSettled` call on the same `Link` replaces the first callback without any warning, so only the last caller gets told. `startSession` calls `whenSettled` every time it runs. That means two sessions started on one `Link` would share this one slot. The field starts out as `null`, which means no callback is registered.

The old `Link` stored no state. Its only field was `transport`, and its `connect` just passed through to `transport.open`. The new version adds two pieces of state per instance: `onSettled`, and an `attempts` counter that the next step's loop uses. The constructor also takes a new `maxAttempts` parameter, which defaults to 3 and sets how many times that loop calls `transport.open` before it gives up.

details.sv:
`settle` is the only other code that touches `onSettled`. It reads the callback and resets the field to `null` (step W1.4). So once a callback has been used, it is gone, and a later `connect` on the same `Link` has nothing to call back unless `whenSettled` runs again first.

Neither revision contains a `new Link(...)` call. So it isn't possible to tell from this code which `maxAttempts` callers actually pass. Any caller that passes only `transport` gets the default of 3.

title.sv: connect tries to open, and the transport succeeds
title.en: connect tries to open, and the transport succeeds

summary.sv: The loop resets the attempt counter, opens the transport, and on success settles and returns 'connected'.
summary.en: The loop resets the attempt counter, opens the transport, and on success settles and returns 'connected'.

body.sv:
Here the walk is inside `link.connect(address)`, which `startSession` is awaiting. The old `connect` simply passed the result of `transport.open` through as a `boolean`. The new `connect`, under the same name, retries in a loop and returns an `Outcome`. It also settles the link, which triggers the callback that `startSession` registered.

On this path, `connect` resets `attempts` to 0, counts the first attempt, and awaits `transport.open`. When `open` is `true`, it calls `settle('connected')` and returns `'connected'` right away. On success, then, the loop runs only once.

Two consequences matter for the review:

- **`attempts` belongs to the `Link` instance, not to one call.** If `connect` is called again on the same `Link` while an earlier call is still waiting on `open` or `pause`, the new call resets the counter for both calls. The earlier call can then make more attempts than `maxAttempts`. Both calls also settle into the same single `onSettled` slot from step W1.2.
- **If `transport.open` rejects, `settle` never runs.** The error leaves `connect`, and `startSession` rejects with it, without reporting anything. The settled callback stays in `onSettled`, so a later `connect` on that `Link` that does settle would fire it.

The next step shows what `settle` does with the callback.

title.sv: settle takes the callback once and schedules it
title.en: settle takes the callback once and schedules it

summary.sv: settle clears onSettled and schedules the callback with setTimeout(0) instead of calling it.
summary.en: settle clears onSettled and schedules the callback with setTimeout(0) instead of calling it.

body.sv:
This step comes from `this.settle('connected')` in the success branch of `connect`. `settle` takes the callback out of `onSettled` and clears the field in the same synchronous step, so a registered callback is scheduled at most once. If `onSettled` is already `null`, for example because no callback was registered or an earlier settle used it, nothing happens.

**`settle` doesn't call the callback; it only queues it with `setTimeout(..., 0)`.** The timer callback runs in a later event-loop task, after the current call stack and all pending promise continuations have finished. `settle` returns right away, and `connect` returns `'connected'` before `'session ready'` has been reported. The callback then runs on its own, outside `connect` and `startSession`. Step W1.6 follows it there.
body.en:

If `onSettled` is already `null`, for example because no callback was registered or an earlier settle used it, nothing happens.

**`settle` doesn't call the callback; it only queues it with `setTimeout(..., 0)`.** The timer callback runs in a later event-loop task, after the current call stack and all pending promise continuations have finished. `settle` returns right away, and `connect` returns `'connected'` before `'session ready'` has been reported. The callback then runs on its own, outside `connect` and `startSession`. Step W1.6 follows it there.

details.sv:
Because the callback runs from a timer, an exception it throws (one thrown by `report`, for example) does not reach `connect` or `startSession`. Whatever awaits `startSession` can't catch it, and it surfaces as an uncaught error in the timer's context.

Clearing `onSettled` only covers the callback that was registered at the moment `settle` ran. If `whenSettled` runs again before the timer fires, the new callback is stored for a later settle. The already-queued call still runs with the old callback, because it captured that callback in its local `callback` variable.

title.sv: Back in startSession: nothing to report yet
title.en: Back in startSession: nothing to report yet

summary.sv: The await resumes with 'connected', the gave-up check does not apply, and startSession finishes.
summary.en: The await resumes with 'connected', the gave-up check does not apply, and startSession finishes.

body.sv:
`connect` has returned `'connected'`, so the `await` in `startSession` resumes with that value. The `'gave-up'` check doesn't apply, so `startSession` reports nothing itself and its promise resolves.

**At this point, `'session ready'` has not been reported yet.** The `await` resumes in a promise continuation (a microtask), and microtasks run before the timer task that `settle` queued in step W1.4. Code that awaits `startSession` therefore continues before the session is reported as ready. The next step follows that timer.

summary.sv: On a later event-loop task, the registered callback runs and reports 'session ready'.
summary.en: On a later event-loop task, the registered callback runs and reports 'session ready'.

body.sv:
This is the same line as in step W1.1, but this time its callback body runs. Nothing in the walk so far calls it. The `setTimeout` queued in `settle` (step W1.4) triggers it in its own event-loop task, after the call stack of `connect` and `startSession` has finished. The callback receives `'connected'`, so the ternary picks `'session ready'` and passes it to `report`.

By this point, `startSession`'s promise has already resolved. Its remaining work after `connect` ran as microtasks, and microtasks all run before the next timer task. **So a caller that awaits `startSession` and assumes `'session ready'` has already been reported is wrong.** Any code that continues right after that `await` runs before the report.

title.sv: A failed open leads to a pause
title.en: A failed open leads to a pause

summary.sv: When open returns false, connect waits attempts × 100 ms and loops again.
summary.en: When open returns false, connect waits attempts × 100 ms and loops again.

body.sv:
This walk goes back to the loop in `connect` from step W1.3, at the `if (open)` branch, and this time `transport.open` returns `false`. `connect` then skips `settle` and the return, and awaits `pause(this.attempts * 100)`. Since `attempts` has just been incremented, the wait grows linearly with each attempt: 100, 200 and 300 ms with the default `maxAttempts` of 3.

**The pause comes before the loop condition is checked again, so the last failed attempt is also followed by a pause.** With the defaults, the third failure still waits 300 ms before the loop ends and `connect` gives up. That last wait retries nothing; it only delays the give-up. In total, `connect` spends 600 ms in pauses, plus however long the three `open` calls take.

The next step shows how `pause` waits.

title.sv: pause wraps a timer in a promise
title.en: pause wraps a timer in a promise

summary.sv: A small helper that resolves after the given number of milliseconds.
summary.en: A small helper that resolves after the given number of milliseconds.

body.sv:
`pause` is a small helper that returns a promise and resolves it from a `setTimeout`. When `connect` awaits it, `connect` gives control back to the event loop and continues only after the timer fires. The wait blocks nothing else.

**So other code can run on the same `Link` while `connect` is paused.** For example, a second `connect` call would reset the shared `attempts` counter (step W1.3), and a new `whenSettled` would replace the callback in `onSettled` (step W1.2). The paused call resumes with whatever state that code left behind.

title.sv: The loop ends: settle 'gave-up' and return it
title.en: The loop ends: settle 'gave-up' and return it

summary.sv: After maxAttempts failures, connect settles with 'gave-up' and returns 'gave-up'.
summary.en: After maxAttempts failures, connect settles with 'gave-up' and returns 'gave-up'.

body.sv:
After the last pause, the loop checks its condition again. `attempts` has reached `maxAttempts`, so the loop ends. `connect` calls `settle('gave-up')`, the same `settle` as in step W1.4: it takes the callback out of `onSettled` and only queues it with a timer. Then `connect` returns `'gave-up'`.

**As in the success case, the callback has not run when `connect` returns.** `startSession` sees the result first, as the next step shows.

summary.sv: The settled callback runs later and reports 'offline mode'.

body.sv:
This is the settled callback from step W1.6, now triggered by the timer that `settle` queued for `'gave-up'`. It runs in its own event-loop task, after `startSession` has already resolved. The outcome isn't `'connected'`, so the ternary picks `'offline mode'`.

As step W2.4 showed, nothing retries. The reviewer has to decide whether these two messages, in this order, are what the change intends.
